First published in Tabl. Encycl. 1: 63 (1791)

This species is accepted

### Editorial Note

This species was treated by Bean in synonymy with Callianthe vexillaria (É.Morren) Donnell (syn. Abutilon vexillarium É.Morren), a situation that obtained until very recently (see e.g. Donnell, Ballard & Cantino 2012). However, the two are now regarded as separate species.

The text below is derived from Bean, with updated taxonomy but otherwise unedited.

An evergreen shrub of lax, graceful habit, to 6 ft high. Leaves ovate, cordate at the base, 2 to 4 in. long, slender-pointed, coarsely toothed. Flowers pendulous, borne singly in the leaf-axils from April onwards; calyx inflated, rich red, about 1 in. long; corolla yellow, about 1⁄2 in. longer than the calyx. The stamens and stigmas form a club-shaped stalked cluster that stands out well beyond the corolla. Bot. Mag., t. 5717.

Native of Brazil. Although by no means hardy, it will survive most winters on a warm, sheltered wall, and is certainly one of the most attractive subjects for such a situation.

Introduced 1860s see Flore des Serres 15

Callianthe megapotamica is a shrub of lax, graceful habit, fantastic when trained against a warm wall. Bayonne Botanic Garden, France. 7 July 2017. Image Guillaume Mamdy.

Leaves of Callianthe megapotamica are ovate, cordate at the base, slender-pointed and coarsely toothed. Bayonne Botanic Garden, France. 7 July 2017. Image Guillaume Mamdy.

Callianthe megapotamica flowering well on a south-facing wall at Coleton Fishacre, on the South Devon coast, UK (14th September 2021). Image Julian Sutton.

Callianthe megapotamica at the JC Raulston Arboretum, North Carolina, USA (4 November 2025), where it forms a free-standing thicket. Image John Grimshaw.


### 'Variegata'

A brightly, blotchily, yellow-variegated clone, created in the 1860s by Lemoine, who grafted the well-known contagious C. striata ‘Thompsonii’ onto C. megapotamica with the inevitable result that Abutilon mosaic virus was transmitted (Reid 1914). Bean (1914) thought that the leaves were ‘charmingly blotched and tessellated with bright yellow’; G.S. Thomas (1992) considered the variegation ‘a doubtful advantage.’

Callianthe megapotamica 'Variegata' trained against a fence in York, UK, still flowering prolifically through the gloom of December (2021). Image John Grimshaw.

### Morphology

The plant is a suffruticose, mat-forming perennial characterized by stems that range from prostrate to erect, emerging from a branched base and reaching up to 30 cm in height. The stems exhibit a hirsute texture. Leaves measure between 1.5 and 2.5 cm in length and vary from lanceolate to ovate in shape; their surfaces range from scabrous to pilose, with notable pubescence concentrated at the base of the lamina. The bracts are typically broader than the leaves and are sessile. The inflorescence is capitate, consisting of densely flowered verticillasters. The calyx is straight, narrowly tubular, and measures 6–7 mm, with dense hirsuteness externally and a ring of hairs on the inner surface at the base of the calyx teeth. The corolla is bilabiate with a notched upper lip, purple in color, measuring 10–12 mm, and is hirsute on its outer surface. The corolla tube, measuring 5–6 mm, is enclosed within the calyx. Both stamens and style are exserted; there are two fertile stamens with adherent anthers. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Description
    

Brazilian bellflower is a showy, deciduous to semi-evergreen, medium-sized, perennial shrub in the mallow family (Malvaceae), native to Brazil. It thrives in subtropical regions and may be grown as an indoor plant or outdoors in a sheltered location. It may reach up to 8 feet tall and has triangular-shaped green leaves and pendulous, bell-shaped, or lantern-like flowers with yellow petals and red calyx. They resemble Chinese lanterns and adorn the shrub with a profusion of blooms from summer until the first frost.
